extracted.intended_audience: researchers, academic authors, journal editors, and research-integrity stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing how journals detect, communicate about, and act on clear cases of plagiarism (including timeliness, admissions, and accountability). Useful for authors, editors, and integrity advocates tracking retraction outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of plagiarism (copied figures and similar text)
rubrics_metrics.description: The allegedly plagiarized article "contained several figures copied from Pineda’s 2020 paper ... as well as similar text."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identification of verbatim or substantially similar text and duplicated figures is core evidence for plagiarism. Such concrete overlaps constitute a 'clear case of plagiarism' that should trigger editorial investigation and correction/retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal obligation to retract clear plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor-in-chief told Pineda he’d retract the article (and said three papers would be retracted for plagiarizing their work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When plagiarism is clear from the evidence, journals are expected to issue retractions rather than leaving plagiarized content in the literature. An editor's promise to retract signals an obligation to follow through with formal correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: A year after the editor promised retractions, the articles remained intact; the publisher blamed the delay on staffing changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retractions and other corrective actions should be conducted promptly. Long delays (months to a year) are problematic; staffing changes are an insufficient justification for excessive delay because they leave the literature uncorrected and aggrieved authors frustrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author admission should expedite action
rubrics_metrics.description: The corresponding author 'accepted his mistake and expressed a strong apology, promising that something like that will never happen in future.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When authors admit plagiarism or error, journals should use that admission to expedite correction or retraction procedures rather than treating it as a reason to delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and fairness across journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Some authors reported that 'papers in other journals [by ur Rehman] were retracted immediately' while these remain intact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial responses should be consistent and fair across journals; inconsistent handling (immediate retractions in some venues but not others) undermines trust in the publishing system and raises questions about selective enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial responsibility and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment: 'The Editor is more responsible as compared to the author. The Editors are more interested in Money Making Game than Plagiarism and Quality of the work submitted.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and publishers bear primary responsibility for maintaining publication integrity. Expectations include proactive investigation, enforcement of policies, and prioritizing quality over commercial or other interests; failure to act is a breach of editorial duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and communication about the retraction process
rubrics_metrics.description: Elsevier said 'We are aware of these papers and the retraction process is indeed underway,' adding that 'journal staffing developments presented some delays.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should provide clear, specific updates on the status and expected timeline of investigations/retractions. Vague statements about staffing or unspecified delays are inadequate; transparent communication helps maintain trust and informs affected parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of community reporting and public pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Pineda posted on LinkedIn asking fellow researchers for advice, and that public post prompted further correspondence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public reporting (social media, posts by aggrieved authors) and community pressure can draw attention to unresolved cases and sometimes prompt action. However, publicizing disputes can have reputational consequences and is often a last-resort mechanism when formal channels stall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of independent tracking and reporting resources (Retraction Watch)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction Watch invites readers to report retractions not in their database and provides a repository of retraction information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent databases and watchdog organizations are valuable for documenting and escalating unresolved integrity issues. Authors and readers should report missing retractions and use these resources to track outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm to scientific integrity from inaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Pineda: 'It is deeply disappointing to see that some scientific journals disregard both the integrity of science and the efforts of those who contribute honestly to the field.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to correct the record damages the scientific enterprise, harms honest contributors, and diminishes confidence in published literature. Timely, decisive corrective action is essential to protect integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corresponding author's duty to request retraction and be aware of rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Ur Rehman emailed Pineda to say he had also requested retraction of the paper and was unaware of the 'many plagiarism rules.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corresponding authors are expected to understand publication ethics and to request or cooperate with retraction/correction when misconduct or errors occur. Lack of awareness is not a substitute for taking corrective steps.
